title: Four places
hook: the places of the birth, awakening, first sermon and passing, worth seeing with devotion

segments.voice: Yesterday: four great references, and your line, set the words beside the discourses. Did you trace a quote back to its source? Today, a worry about the future, and four places on a map. Day five hundred forty-nine.

The Buddha is lying between the twin sal trees at Kusinara now, near the end. And Ananda raises a practical worry. Until now, he says, at the end of every rainy season, monks from all over came to see the Blessed One, and we got to see them, and learn from them. When you're gone, we won't have that. Where will people go? Underneath it sits a plainer question: where do we go now, to feel close? The Buddha's answer is very concrete. Today: four places.
screen: `BETWEEN THE SAL TREES.` → `WHERE WILL PEOPLE GO?` → `A CONCRETE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: There are four places, Ananda, that a person of faith should see, places that stir the heart. The Pali word is samvejaniya: stirring, moving. The first: here the Tathagata was born. The second: here the Tathagata awakened to full awakening. The third: here the Tathagata set the wheel of the Dhamma rolling. The fourth: here the Tathagata passed into final nibbana. The sutta itself doesn't name the towns. It simply says here, here, here, here. Tradition has filled in the map: Lumbini, in what is now Nepal; Bodh Gaya, under the tree; the deer park at Isipatana near Varanasi, now called Sarnath; and Kusinara, where he is lying as he speaks. Then he adds that monks and nuns, laymen and laywomen, will come to these places, and whoever dies on such a pilgrimage with a heart at peace will be reborn in a good destination. It's a startling moment. A teacher who spent his life pointing people inward, to the breath and the mind, also says: go and stand there. The places don't hold magic in the text. They hold the four turning points of one life: arriving, waking up, sharing it, letting go. Pilgrims still travel between them.
screen: `SAMVEJANIYA: PLACES THAT STIR.` · `BORN, AWAKENED, TAUGHT, PASSED.` · `THE SUTTA ONLY SAYS HERE.` · `GO AND STAND THERE.` · then, large: `FOUR PLACES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and picture the four places one at a time. A grove where a child is born. A tree where a man sits until he understands. A deer park where five friends listen. Two sal trees where an old man lies down. Give each one a few breaths. Then, if you like, picture four places in your own life: where you began, where something woke up in you, where you first shared it, and where you let something go. The bell holds the time.
Four places. Birth, awakening, the first teaching and the final passing: the four places the Buddha said are worth seeing, places that stir the heart. Today's word.
Your line: places that stir the heart. Today, when you pass a place that matters to you, slow down for one breath and let it stir you. Day five hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhists from across Asia and the world make pilgrimage to Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar, often visiting all four on one journey, chanting, meditating and making offerings at each.

myth: DN 16 names Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kusinara by name
the sutta says only 'here the Tathagata was born', and so on; tradition supplies the names.

places that shake the heart awake.

fork.setup: you're Ananda. your teacher is dying. you worry that people will have nowhere to go to feel close to him. what does he tell you?
options: visit four places: his birth, awakening, first teaching and passing.
build one great temple in his name.
fork.reveal: he names four places worth seeing with devotion, places that stir the heart.

original.note: Pali samvejaniya: stirring, moving. the four places are samvejaniya thana, places that stir.

trapdoor: what you thought: pilgrimage came later, after the early teaching.
what it means: in DN 16 the Buddha himself names four places worth seeing with a moved heart.
what a scholar hears: the four samvejaniya-thanas are unnamed in the sutta; an Ashokan pillar inscription at Lumbini (Rummindei) records a royal visit to the birthplace.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), the four places that stir the heart

notes: DN 16 paraphrased. Confirm the passage comes while the Buddha lies at Kusinara, and that the four places are not named in the sutta text.
The Ashokan Rummindei pillar inscription at Lumbini (c. 249 BCE) is in the scholar floor; confirm the dating phrasing 'third century BCE'.
Rebirth in a good destination for those who die on pilgrimage with a confident heart: confirm wording (sugati, sagga).

Editor review (2026-10-01): removed a line telling the listener what they feel, the two-thousand-years date and an empty uplift line; trapdoor drops the BCE date and says the Ashokan inscription records a royal visit.
